turns.content: Okay, so I finally heard back from two more beta readers this week — Priya Ramanathan and Marcus Holloway. I've read both letters twice and I'm still sitting with them. Can I just walk you through what they said before we dig in? I want to make sure I'm not reacting too fast in either direction.

Please do. Walk me through both letters at your own pace. It's worth taking the time to lay them out clearly before you start deciding what to do with the feedback. Beta letters are strange documents — they compress a reader's entire experience of your novel into a few pages, and the impulse to react immediately, either defensively or by agreeing with everything, is usually the wrong one. Start with whichever letter you want to talk through first.

I'll start with Priya Ramanathan. She's in my writing group and she reads very carefully — she's the kind of person who flags things like comma splices in workshop, which can be annoying but also means I trust her at the sentence level. Her overall response was positive. She said the novel's emotional core held, and that Eleanor's relationship with Camille was the strongest thing in the manuscript. But she had two specific critiques. The first is that chapter 7 felt expository in the dialogue. Her exact note was something like, 'the characters are explaining the backstory to each other in a way that neither character would actually need explained to them.' I know exactly which scene she means — it's the kitchen conversation where Eleanor and Camille are going over what happened with the house after Iris died. The second thing Priya caught was an anachronism. She flagged the word 'doomscroll' appearing in a 1965 journal entry. One of Grandmother Iris Penhallow's entries from 1965 — I must have written that line very late at night because I have no memory of putting it there, but she's absolutely right. 'Doomscroll' didn't exist in 1965. That has to go.

Both of Priya's notes are worth acting on, but they're different in kind and deserve different responses.

The 'doomscroll' anachronism in the 1965 journal entry is a clear-cut fix. That's the kind of error that pulls a careful reader completely out of the historical texture of Iris's voice, and it needs to be corrected before the manuscript goes anywhere else. The good news is that it's surgical — you find the word, you replace it with something period-appropriate, and it's done. What's Iris describing in that entry? If you tell me the context, I can think with you about what language she might actually have used in 1965 to describe whatever feeling or behavior 'doomscroll' was standing in for.

The chapter 7 dialogue critique is more interesting and requires more thought before you act on it. Priya is describing what's usually called 'as-you-know-Bob' dialogue — characters explaining things to each other that they both already know, for the benefit of the reader. The fact that she can feel it means it's working against the scene rather than for it. But the reason that scene probably exists is that the reader genuinely does need the information. The question isn't whether to cut the information; it's whether there's a way to get it onto the page that doesn't require Eleanor and Camille to have a conversation that no two sisters who'd lived through the same events would actually have. Do you remember what information you were trying to deliver in that scene? That's the starting point.

The Iris journal context — in that 1965 entry she's writing about a habit she had of reading the newspaper obsessively, looking for news that confirmed her worst fears about the world. So 'doomscroll' was doing real thematic work there, but it obviously can't stay. Maybe something like 'she would rifle through the pages looking for disaster' — I don't know, I'll work on it.

On chapter 7: yes, exactly. The information Eleanor and Camille are delivering to each other in chapter 7 is basically the history of what happened to the house after Iris died — who handled the estate, when things got sold off, how Brent Halloran first came into the picture. I think I put it in dialogue because I panicked about pacing. A straight flashback felt too slow, so I had them talk through it instead, and Priya's right that it lands as expository. I'm wondering if some of that backstory could be carried through Iris's journal entries instead — spread the house history across a few entries rather than dumping it in one kitchen scene.

The Iris solution you just described — rifling through pages looking for disaster — is actually stronger than 'doomscroll' would be even if 'doomscroll' were period-appropriate. It's more concrete, it's more Iris's voice, and it does the same thematic work without leaning on a contemporary shorthand. That's a genuine improvement, not just a fix.

On chapter 7: the instinct to route that backstory through Iris's journal entries is a good one, and here's why it solves the structural problem rather than just relocating it. The reason the kitchen dialogue feels expository is that Eleanor and Camille are too close to this history — it would be strange for them to narrate it to each other. But Iris writing in her journal in real time, recording her fears about what might happen to the house, what she hoped for, what she worried about — that's not exposition, that's character. The reader would receive the same information, but now it arrives with emotional weight rather than information-delivery weight. The challenge is that Iris's journal entries are dated 1962 to 1971, so you'd need to find entries that fall in the right window to plant the relevant history. Is there already a journal entry near the end of that run — say 1969 or 1970 — where Iris might plausibly be thinking about what will happen to the house after she's gone? That feels like the natural place to seed the Brent Halloran backstory without it feeling forced.

There's an entry from 1970 where Iris is writing about the land taxes going up and feeling like the house is becoming a burden she can't carry. That's actually perfect — I could expand that entry to include some of her anxieties about what happens if she can't keep it, which would set up everything about Brent Halloran coming in later without any of it needing to be stated in dialogue. I feel better about this. Let me tell you what Marcus said, because his letter is a different kind of challenge.

Marcus Holloway is less interested in the sentence level and more interested in what he calls 'the architecture of the emotional experience.' He's a literary fiction guy who reads a lot of theory, which makes his feedback feel a bit abstract sometimes, but when he's right, he's really right. He said two things that I'm still sitting with. The first is that he thought Owen Trask was the strongest minor character in the manuscript — stronger than he needed to be for the role he plays. Marcus's note was that Owen Trask has a specificity and a stillness that most of the other supporting characters don't quite reach, and that the novel might be underleveraging him. The second thing Marcus said was that he wanted an ambiguous ending rather than the reconciliation I have planned for Eleanor and Camille. His argument was that the ambiguous ending would be more honest to how estrangement actually works. And then — like Priya — he flagged Brent Halloran as cartoonish. He used that exact word.

Both Priya and Marcus landing on Brent Halloran being cartoonish is a signal you can't ignore. When two readers from different orientations — Priya at the sentence level, Marcus at the architectural level — arrive at the same word independently, that's not a coincidence. It's a convergent finding, and it means Halloran as currently written is failing on multiple levels at once: not just stylistically but structurally. The developer-as-antagonist is a type that carries a lot of baggage in literary fiction about land and inheritance, and if Halloran reads as cartoonish, it's probably because he's functioning as a symbol rather than a person. What do you actually know about him as a character? What does he want beyond the obvious, and what does he think about himself?

On the Marcus notes separately: his Owen Trask observation is interesting. The instinct when a minor character outshines the supporting cast is to either expand their role or worry that you've spent energy in the wrong place. But I'd push back gently on the idea that Owen Trask being the strongest minor character is necessarily a problem. Sometimes the minor characters are stronger precisely because you weren't trying as hard with them — there's an ease and specificity that comes from writing someone without the weight of plot necessity on them. Marcus might be right that Owen is underleveraged, or he might be responding to the quality of that particular characterization and generalizing it into a structural suggestion. What role does Owen currently play in the novel, and does expanding it change anything about the story you're actually trying to tell?

And then the ambiguous ending: I want to hear more about what your planned reconciliation looks like before I say anything about whether Marcus's advocacy for an ambiguous ending is worth taking seriously. What happens between Eleanor and Camille at the end of the manuscript right now?

Brent Halloran — you're right that he's functioning as a symbol. I think I've been using him as a vessel for everything I find threatening about development culture and real estate speculation, and it's showing. He doesn't have an inner life. He shows up, he makes offers, he applies pressure, he doesn't listen. I know that's a failure. But I'm also not sure I want to spend a lot of time making him sympathetic. He doesn't need to be the protagonist of his own story, he just needs to stop being a cardboard villain.

Owen Trask is currently in four scenes. He builds wooden boats in a converted barn outside Stonington, he has one long conversation with Eleanor in chapter 9 where he talks about what it means to build something that will outlast you, and he's present in two shorter scenes where he's more peripheral. The chapter 9 scene is the one Marcus is responding to, I'm sure of it — it's the scene I'm proudest of in the whole manuscript. But giving Owen Trask more space would mean taking space from something else, and I don't know what.

On the ending: right now, Eleanor and Camille have a conversation in the last chapter where they make a kind of partial peace. It's not a full reconciliation — it's more like they acknowledge what happened and agree to try. I deliberately left it short of a resolution. Marcus wants me to go further into ambiguity — he thinks even that partial acknowledgment is more closure than the material earns. And honestly? Part of me agrees with him. But part of me thinks the readers who've been with Eleanor for 81,200 words deserve something.

Let's take these one at a time.

On Brent Halloran: the distinction you're drawing — he doesn't need to be sympathetic, he just needs to stop being cardboard — is exactly the right frame. You don't owe him interiority for its own sake. But even a character who is genuinely in the wrong can have legible human motivations that make him feel real rather than functional. The question to ask is: what does Brent Halloran tell himself about what he's doing? Not what the novel knows about him, but what he knows about himself. If you can answer that in one sentence — even privately, even in your notes, never on the page — it will change how he moves through scenes. Cartoonish villains are people who don't believe they're doing anything wrong but the author hasn't figured out their internal justification yet. Give him one. It doesn't have to be convincing, it just has to be his.

On Owen Trask: don't expand his role based on Marcus's note. Marcus liked him, and that's meaningful information, but 'the strongest minor character' is a description, not a prescription. Owen Trask works because he has exactly as much space as he needs — the chapter 9 scene you're proudest of is probably the reason. Adding more Owen scenes won't make Owen better; it'll make Owen the same quality spread thinner. The note to take from Marcus on Owen Trask is really just: whatever you did there, understand it and see if you can bring it to the other supporting characters.

On the ending: this is the hardest call, and I want to be honest with you about it. The ambiguous ending Marcus is advocating for is probably the more artistically defensible choice. But that doesn't mean it's the right choice for this novel. The question isn't whether ambiguity is truer to how estrangement actually works — Marcus is probably right that it is. The question is what kind of novel you set out to write, and whether the 81,200 words that precede the ending have built toward partial acknowledgment or toward open-ended silence. What does your gut say when you imagine cutting even that partial peace from the ending?

My gut says I'd grieve it. Which might mean it's earned, or it might mean I'm too attached to it. I honestly can't tell from the inside. But I think what I'm hearing from you is that I shouldn't let Marcus's advocacy for an ambiguous ending push me into a structural change I'm not sure about. Is that right?

The Brent Halloran note is landing. 'What does he tell himself about what he's doing' — that's the question I haven't answered yet. I think if I could write one paragraph from his point of view — just for myself, not for the manuscript — it might unlock something.

I want to step back and do a kind of triage pass with you. Between what Priya said and what Marcus said, I have: the 'doomscroll' anachronism fix, the chapter 7 restructure, the Halloran characterization, the question of Owen Trask's role, and the ending. Those are five things. I'm going to have to prioritize. What would you put in the 'do this now' column versus the 'think longer' column?

Yes, that's right. Don't let Marcus's advocacy for an ambiguous ending move you on its own. One reader's strongly held preference about endings is data, not a directive. If a second or third reader comes back with the same note, the picture changes. Right now it's one voice, and the grief you'd feel cutting the partial acknowledgment is itself meaningful information.

Here's the triage.

Do this now: The 'doomscroll' fix in the 1965 journal entry. This is a clean error with a clean solution, and you already have a better line. Do it today before anything else. There's no reason to sit on it. The Brent Halloran paragraph — not a revision, just a private note you write for yourself about his internal justification. This is low cost and high leverage. It might unlock nothing; it might change how every Halloran scene reads on the next pass.

Do this in the next revision pass: The chapter 7 restructure, routing that backstory through Iris's journal entries. You've already identified the right entry — the 1970 land tax passage. This is more involved but you have a clear plan. It's not urgent today but it belongs in the next substantive revision.

Think longer: Owen Trask's role. Do not expand it until you understand clearly what you'd be trading away, and until you're confident the Marcus note is about structure rather than just the quality of that one scene. Sit with it through the rest of the beta round. The ending. Keep it provisional. See what the other readers say — you mentioned five beta readers, and you heard from Davinia Okafor first in your last session with notes about Eleanor's profession feeling thin. Wait for the remaining letters before you make any decisions about structure at that scale. Endings deserve the full picture.

That triage makes sense to me. Fix the anachronism today, write the Halloran paragraph for myself, plan the chapter 7 revision, and hold the Owen Trask and ending questions until I've heard from everyone. I think I've been treating all five things as equally urgent, which is part of why I've been spinning on this since the letters arrived. Breaking it into 'do now' and 'think longer' is useful.

One last thing before we close — both Priya and Marcus flagged Brent Halloran as cartoonish, and I keep coming back to that overlap. Is there something structurally going on with villain characters in literary fiction about land and place that makes this a common failure? Because I don't think I'm the only writer who's made this mistake.

You're definitely not the only writer who's made it. The developer-as-antagonist is one of the most common figures in contemporary literary fiction about place, inheritance, and environmental threat, and it almost always produces the same failure mode. Here's why.

Developers in real life are motivated by a combination of financial incentive, genuine belief in their own contribution, and a particular way of understanding land that treats value as exchangeable and improvable. They are not, in their own minds, villains. But in fiction about a place that the novel clearly loves — a coastline, an inherited house, a community — the author's sympathies are so legible that the developer tends to get written from the outside rather than from the inside. He becomes the embodiment of what threatens the novel's values rather than a person who holds a different set of values. When that happens, Brent Halloran stops being a character and starts being a function. Readers feel it as cartoonish because on some level they can see the author's hand.

The writers who solve this problem usually solve it the same way: they give the developer something the protagonists lack. Not something sympathetic, necessarily. Something real. In your case, Brent Halloran might have a clearer understanding of the financial reality of the house than Eleanor does — he might be right, in his terms, about what the property is worth and what's going to happen to it regardless of what Eleanor wants. He doesn't have to be right about what matters. But he has to be right about something. That's usually what transforms a cartoonish antagonist into a genuinely unsettling one — the moment when the reader has to acknowledge that he's not entirely wrong, even while everything he represents is exactly what the novel is arguing against.

The paragraph you're going to write for yourself about his internal justification is the right place to find that. What does Brent Halloran think he's saving Eleanor from?

That last question — 'what does Brent Halloran think he's saving Eleanor from' — is the most useful thing anyone has said to me about this novel in weeks. I'm going to write that paragraph tonight. Thank you. I feel significantly less overwhelmed than I did when I opened this session.

Good. Go write the paragraph while the question is still live in your mind — that's the right moment for it.

You came in with five things and a lot of noise, and you're leaving with a clear order of operations: the 'doomscroll' fix today, the Brent Halloran paragraph tonight, the chapter 7 restructure in the next revision pass, and the Owen Trask and ending questions held in reserve until the remaining beta letters arrive. That's not a small thing. Half of what makes a revision go wrong is working on everything at once.

The fact that Priya Ramanathan and Marcus Holloway both landed on Brent Halloran being cartoonish — with Priya coming at it from the sentence level and Marcus from the architectural level — means you have a real thing to fix, and you now have a way into it. The rest is time and attention. Come back when the other letters arrive.
